claims.text: A refractory high-entropy alloy containing sufficient Nb and Ta and forming a homogeneous BCC phase can exhibit superconductivity at cryogenic temperatures.
Nb and Ta are superconducting elements.
The superconducting pairing interactions associated with Nb and Ta can be preserved when those elements form part of a refractory HEA solid solution.
An as-cast HEA containing W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V can display a predominantly homogeneous BCC phase.
Cooling the alloy below its critical temperature can induce its superconducting state.
Low external magnetic fields help avoid suppression of superconductivity.
A coherent BCC structure and uniform elemental distribution minimize phase segregation.
A coherent BCC structure and uniform elemental distribution minimize disruption of electron pairing.
The d-electron states of Nb and Ta facilitate superconducting pairing in the HEA.
Nb and Ta incorporated into a high-entropy matrix can sustain Cooper pairing if their electronic states remain sufficiently coherent despite lattice distortion.
Below a critical temperature, the alloy should exhibit zero electrical resistance.
Below a critical temperature, the alloy should exhibit a clear Meissner effect.
At room temperature, the as-cast alloy behaves as a normal metal with finite resistivity.
Superconductivity requires a sufficiently high concentration and homogeneous distribution of Nb and Ta together with a stable BCC microstructure.
Significant secondary phases or the absence of Nb and Ta may prevent superconductivity in these HEAs.
